t: Levels of Consensus
q: Consensus is not agreement. Reaching consensus in a group means everyone can live with the decision or choice.
Too many teams continue to discuss decisions and issues where consensus already exists.
Levels of Consensus is one such device that is used widely in effective organizations.
Expressing a level is not a vote but a measure of conviction at a given point in time.
Using the Levels of Consensus tool to test where the group stands on an issue before a discussion can save valuable time.

t: How Can We Improve Our Judgment
q: Good judgment comes from experience and experience comes from bad judgment, or so goes the well-known quote.
Technically speaking, judgment is the ability to weigh complex information and competing ideas and reach a reasonable conclusion.
This is why people with strong convictions, committed ideologies, and deep-seated assumptions often make poor judgments.
People with poor judgment often limit the possibilities too quickly or land on a viewpoint before considering the options.
Our judgment evolves as we open the mind before narrowing it.

t: The Good, the Bad & the Ugly Behind the Desire for Promotion
q: The desire for the next role and a deserved promotion to a more senior leadership position seems to be a natural motivation in organizational life.
Not everyone who accepts an elevated role does so with positive intentions.
People who covet promotion solely for more compensation or for status make for ineffectual leaders.
The ugliest justification for promotion isn’t as bad as it is self-destructive.
As the poet T.S. Eliot so aptly noted, the greatest treason is “To do the right deed for the wrong reason.

t: The 10 Most Important Teaching & Learning Studies of the Last 50 Years
q: He found that roughly seven items could be recalled in normal adults, give or take two. While this number has since been re-investigated, this finding ultimately proved the limited capacity of working memory.
This shows that when teachers have high expectations, they subconsciously alter their behaviours to be more supportive, allowing student achievement to be maximised.

Retrieval Practice and Spacing emerged as the most effective techniques, benefiting learners of all ages and abilities, and consistently enhancing performance across different tasks and educational settings.
On the other hand, techniques such as summarisation, highlighting, keyword mnemonic, imagery and re-reading ranked lowest in terms of utility and are not recommended as primary learning tools.

An intriguing discovery emerged: after 24 hours of learning, participants experienced a memory boost, remembering more on the morning of the second day than on the night of the first. This improvement was due to the negative impact of fatigue on memory and the restorative power of sleep.

t: Masses of Mistakes: Improving Y11 Revision
q: Some strength training as they carry it home before dumping it somewhere in their room, never to be seen again. They feel as if they achieved something because they possess some ‘revision’ and the teacher feels like things are ok because they gave the pupils lots of work to do.
They complete lots of it, with no idea if it is correct or incorrect. They may well be practising getting it wrong, reinforcing mistakes and misconceptions.

If a pupil really struggles with trigonometry, written work on trig, completed at home with no support, is unlikely to improve their performance. It will probably just make them feel bad, if they can bear to start the work at all.

Annotated working is more valuable than simple mark schemes. You can print it or, to reduce printing, make it available online. This gives them better guidance on what ‘good’ looks like, and a meaningful example to look at if they are stuck.

Past papers or mixed revision hastily cobbled together is unlikely to be valuable. Attempting a past paper when only part-way through the course is demoralising and it teaches pupils it is normal not to try some questions.

t: Attention First
q: All the tasks of the teacher will fail if students aren’t listening. Too often, new teachers are given targets that take them too quickly beyond the fundamental of ensuring student attention.
Silence in 5… everyone pens down looking this way in 4… thank you, James – already there… 3… absolute silence in 2… waiting on 2 students only now… 1… thank you… zero.
As Doug Lemov would say, be seen looking. Crane your neck and move to a place where you can see.
In narrating the positive, the class see that the norm is following instructions, that the teacher isn’t battling against them.
New teachers often feel they have to get to the content – the actual teaching – but we save time in the long-term if we don’t allow a failure to follow instructions.

t: 3-Read Friday #2: Attention, Y11 Revision, and Landmark Teaching Studies
q: I’m obsessed with student attention in lessons, and Pete Foster’s post had me at the first line: All the tasks of the teacher will fail if students aren’t listening.
Pete goes on to share super practical tips to help check and secure student attention throughout a lesson, including when giving instructions and when students are working independently.
Dani returns with a lovely post about the potential pitfalls of a common teacher practice around exam time: giving students loads of printed revision material to take home.
For a research geek like me, this post is heaven. The Inner Drive team reflect on 10 seminal studies that have something important to say about teaching and learning.

We start with Miller’s 1956 study about the limits of working memory that laid the foundations for Cognitive Load Theory, and travel through time to Chen’s 2017 research into metacognition, calling in on studies about forgetting, resilience and mobile phones along the way.

t: The Invisible Power of Trust Between Teammates
q: Many of the most profound influences in life are not visible. Think gravity, magnetic fields, friction, and ultrasound.
Of the many qualities that distinguish high-performing teams, trust is the discriminating X-factor by a wide margin.
Instead of selecting college all-stars, Brooks chose players who had played and competed together for years.
If there is a secret to team chemistry, it might be this: trust depends more on what team members think of each other’s skills than on just about anything else.
It wears a cloak but reveals itself in the threads of high performance.

t: High Potential for What, Exactly
q: Organizations work hard to identify those team members who possess high potential.
The idea of what counts as high potential, however, is rarely debated: Potential for what?
In many cases, those with the label rise quickly through the ranks of leadership even though their skills to lead others is not where they excel.
Not all potential reflects a prowess for leadership. Before deciding who the high potentials are, the best organizations define what they mean and who they are looking for.
Just don’t presume everyone with the ability to do more should become a more senior leader or manager.

t: Admired Leaders Are a Rare Combination of Results and Followership
q: Apparently, Yaccarino earned the label by combining a hard-nosed negotiation style with a warm and relational demeanor.
Identify an iconic leader with a well-known reputation and you will likely identify a results-based leader who has enjoyed tremendous success over many years.
Leaders who share both qualities—results and followership—are exceedingly rare and enjoy an unusual respect from almost everyone around them.
Team members refuse to let such leaders down, going above and beyond because they perceive a meaningful connection to the leader.
We have no idea if the “Velvet Hammer” is one such leader, but her reputation, at least to date, suggests she is operating in the right zip code.

t: Why You Must Stop Giving Fake Grades
q: Teachers giving grades students haven’t earned is rampant, staggering in its increasing frequency.
The result is that an ‘A’ for one student can look very different from an ‘A’ given to another.
The bill will eventually come due. A person can only fake what is falsely written down on paper for so long.
They’re so pumped full of praise and phony appraisal of their abilities that when the truth sets in it’s devastating. Their whole world is upended. Their dreams die.
They have no grit, no toughness, no resiliency. They’ve been given excuses for so long that that’s all they have.
But set your standards in cement. Let your students fail if that’s where they fall. Let them feel disappointment.
It is in the face of hard truth that change happens. It is confrontation with being knocked down that provides the purchase to begin standing back up.

t: The Cost of Consistency
q: But sensible doesn’t mean flawless. It’s easy to tell staff that a new scheme or a new structure will provide benefits for all, but often this just isn’t true.

But I felt different once I was required to take on some responsibility for the quality of teaching across an entire school. Suddenly, my first priority was universal adequacy, even where that placed constraints on the most expert teachers in the school.

There are also subtle gains from consistency that compound: teachers can better support each other, professional development can be better targeted and interventions can build more readily on routines that are familiar to all pupils.

I suspect that the pushback against systematic phonics teaching and detailed curriculum resources, for example, is frequently the conduit through which stifled voices within the profession try to make themselves heard.

We need honest conversations about the compromises that are deemed necessary, ones that will allow us to include on the balance sheet all of those often-hidden items like the demotivation of more experienced colleagues and the potential loss to the profession of their expert presence in the classroom.

t: Manage Expectations to Improve Pre-Observation Conversations https://www.ollielovell.com/tot/141-manage-expectations-to-improve-pre-observation-conversations/
q: We constantly make predictions about what’s coming next, from what time we can leave work, to how much money we expect to find when we check our balance at the ATM.

This is why, in coaching, pre-observation conversations are crucial. It’s isn’t so much how positive, negative, direct or facilitative the messaging is that influences how a coachee takes their feedback.
It sets the expectation that challenge will occur, and it reframes that challenge as meaning that progress is being made, rather than something that’s solely negative.
Rehearsal helps teachers to break unproductive old habits, and to form more productive new ones! But rehearsal is often foreign to coachees.

Showing a video of rehearsal makes it crystal clear to a coachee what that rehearsal will look like. That it’ll be hard work, that I’ll be explicit with my feedback and guidance, but also that we can have a bit of fun with it.

t: Five Ways to Use Worked Examples
q: The worked example effect describes how we can enhance learning "by studying worked examples to problems rather than by trying to solve the original problems" (Ayres, 2012).

Engelmann and Carnine (1991) call this the wording principle: "To make the sequence of examples as clear as possible, use the same wording on juxtaposed examples (or wording that is as similar as possible).
Engelmann and Carnine (1991): "Make sure that the single interpretation emerges as early as possible. It must occur by example 7; however, it should be strongly implied by example 5.

Koedinger, et al. (2023): "a typical student learning a typical KC tends to require seven additional practice opportunities to reach mastery after noninteractive verbal instruction (i.e., text or lecture)

In summary, make the most of your worked examples by: carefully planning a series of examples or how you will modify one to the next, providing or modelling the examples to students, having students explain to themselves what the steps are, pairing an example with a related problem to check for understanding, and simplifying the conditions for students to practice as necessary.

t: 3-Read Friday #1: Pre-Observation Coaching, Consistency, and Worked Examples
q: Ollie offers three super useful suggestions for the conversation that coaches - or anyone who observes a colleague’s lesson - can have before the feedback session to increase the chance of a positive, productive outcome.
I am always interested in the level of autonomy teachers have in the classroom.
In many of the maths departments I support, I feel less autonomy is a price worth paying for greater consistency - for example, insisting staff use certain high-quality resources or approaches.
Chris Such has made me consider a different side to this argument.

I found this post super useful for ideas I can build into my current practice (I initially deliver worked examples in silence using my Silent Teacher approach), but also for ideas about alternate ways to deliver worked examples, such as presenting completed solutions and using maximally different positive examples.

t: Team Leaders Should Not Be the Only Ones With Coaching Assignments
q: Everyone on the team needs the attention of the leader as coach.
Leveraging the entire team and asking each member to play a coaching role is how the best leaders solve this dilemma.
These are not permanent assignments. In fact, most last for only a handful of days or a couple of weeks.
It seems becoming the teacher changes the way a student learns.
The best leaders unlock the wisdom and skills of the collective team so they can unlock the potential of every team member.

t: #23 Wait for Golden Silence
q: As the teacher goes over to these students, even though she speaks really quietly, the volume in the room creeps up and the focus dwindles.
The problem is that when students first settle down to silent, independent work, that silence is incredibly fragile.
It does not take much of a distraction or interruption to shatter it, and then you are fighting to get it back.
If you give the students a bit more time to work in silence, they will be in that place of absorption in the task.
At that point, the silence is strong and robust, and you can give it a little push and it won’t buckle.
I call this kind of silence Golden Silence – when students are quiet and engrossed, and small distractions won’t throw them.
Of course, the path to Golden Silence will be a lot smoother if the behaviour is good, everyone has their equipment, and students know how they should act if they are stuck.

t: How To Stand Like A Leader And Get Respect
q: How you present yourself to your students matters. The way you dress, speak, and move has an impact on how they view you and thus how they behave in your class.
This stance lets people know that you’re committed to your words and have confidence in yourself and what you’re saying. It reflects certainty over uncertainty.
Showing your hands makes you more trustworthy. Moving them to emphasize your points demonstrates warmth and enthusiasm.
Students don’t want to follow a weak-kneed underachiever or someone who stands like one. They have to believe in you.
Researcher Amy Cuddy discovered that if you stand like a superhero for just two minutes, you perform better.
Instead, make it a point to hold a beat of eye contact with all your students throughout each day. The more you do it, the easier it gets and more influence you’ll have.

t: Teams Learn to Ignore Leaders Who Chase Fads
q: They tell everyone about the new insight and begin to rally support behind an idea or program that, if sustained, might add some value.
Team members have seen this movie before, and they know just what to do: Feign interest and wait until this temporary insanity passes.
Faddish leaders hurt their credibility each time they embrace the next new thing.
This makes the leader less believable and is a tremendous waste of time.
Leaders who follow fads usually don’t recognize how many times they have repeated the same pattern.

t: The Norm of Who Gets to Advocate in Team Discussions
q: Norms are shared agreements among team members about which behaviors are valued in the team and which behaviors are not.
Leaving it to the team and its natural process to create norms not only takes too much time, but can also result in dysfunctional norms.
How vigorously a team enforces a norm typically reflects how important they perceive it is to the leader.
A common norm on many teams is to give leaders and those with higher status more airtime.
Anyone with expertise or a strong viewpoint who wants to be heard on a topic will be given the floor and allowed to articulate their views without interruption or disagreement.

t: The Best Reference Anyone Can Receive or Give
q: After serving and receiving many references, leaders soon learn there is an unwritten code to reference-making.
The reference that truly stands out is unusual because it is rarely true.
Endorsers, either by voice or writing, generally follow the same pattern. They establish how well they know the person and highlight the superlative qualities the person has demonstrated.
Leaders who give or receive a reference that flat out suggests the choice that should be made regarding the person wildly shake the tree.
Uncommon conviction, given or received, moves people to action.

t: When Decisions Arent Reversible
q: One-way decisions are those choices that can’t be easily reversed.
Two-way decisions, on the other hand, are those choices that, if need be, can be changed or altered.
By applying a full-blown decision process to all decisions, leaders gum up the works.
By increasing the ownership and autonomy around two-way decisions, leaders empower team members and trust them.
An organization that can’t decide the everyday choice with speed soon becomes bogged down by bureaucracy and red tape.

t: Listening for What Doesnt Get Said
q: He is considered a master of “downforce,” the turbulence created by high cornering speeds.
They listen attentively to what their car tells them from its movements or lack of them.
Instead, they have learned to listen for what isn’t getting said or discussed.
Sometimes, the lack of discussion or advocacy simply means everyone is busy and distracted.
Leaders who miss it often wind up confronting a growing dissent without warning.

t: #22 Ask students to respond in full sentences
q: There is another improvement that could be made, and it is one I rarely see in maths classrooms: the requirement for students to respond in complete sentences.
In the first version of the exchange, the first and second parts of the statement are separated, both by time and additional dialogue.
But when combined with the first part of the statement, we have something that makes sense and is worth remembering.

The way we speak is often very different to the way we write, so if we can promote this more formal way of responding, it could provide a smoother transition for when we ask students to write in full sentences.
A cursory look through any maths GCSE examiner’s report reveals just how much students struggle with questions that ask them to explain, describe and discuss.
In the second version of the exchange, with the question and answer united, Isaac has a better chance of making sense of it.
As with many teaching strategies, it is a good idea to explain to students why you want them to do this.

t: Pride of Craft Is Unequaled Pride
q: Each pair of Cole Haan shoes takes five craftsmen up to 30 hours to produce by hand.
The reason is not how special the company is or the benefits offered to the team.
Those who own the work take the utmost pride in the outcome.
Great leaders know that loyalty springs from the pride of controlling the quality of the products or services being created.
An organization or team filled with people proud of the work they do will stand firm against adversity and challenge.

t: The Sacrifice Every Great Leader Makes
q: To become a truly effective leader, you must be willing to pay the price of leadership success.
The affection, compassion, and commitment expected from leaders are rarely reciprocated by the team.
They presume any leader by definition doesn’t require that kind of attention.
They sacrifice their own need for support and connection by giving even more of it to others.
True leaders suspend their need for support by giving more of it to others.

t: How To Deal With Your Students' Sagging Pants
q: Sagging pants are a problem in the classroom. They’re a problem because they bring an attitude of rebelliousness.
All fine and good. But it’s linked with disrespect. It’s linked with antagonism toward rules, authority, listening, and learning.
Part of being a leader is doing what is right for your students even if they or others disagree.
If you lay it out the first of the year, if you let your students know up front what is expected, then they’ll accept it. Grudgingly perhaps, but they understand.
A teacher who requires non-negotiable standards that are best for students is respected. They’re respected even by the most challenging students who may not respect another adult in their life.
It’s a simple little thing, sagging pants, but like all details, when added up, make a big difference.

t: #21 Don't give exam papers or homework back before whole class feedback
q: All of a sudden students begin obsessing about their marks and the marks of their mates.
Josh has a look through his paper and sees he has got Question 3 correct, and so promptly switches off and starts flicking bits of rubber at Ben.

It is far superior in terms of effectiveness and workload to what I used to do for most of my career: write individual feedback on each student’s work that would take hours and subsequently be ignored.
As soon as you give students their assessments back before diving into whole-class feedback, you lose a lot of time and attention in the ways described above.
Just because students watch you go through how to do a tricky question and then copy it into their books does not mean they understand it.
This follow-up question provides an extra incentive for students to listen hard to your explanation and provides you with some evidence that the explanation you have given makes sense.
